articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny
articles.content_orig:

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology. The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on the relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday. U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia. Historically, China has been a big market for the company. It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives. In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to expand access to China , and some of his persuasion tactics have been successful. Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.
On numerous occasions, Huang has publicly lamented export controls, calling them a “ failure ” at a conference last year and saying in May that it was “ not wise ” for the U.S. and China to create two distinct AI ecosystems. He has also warned that shutting Nvidia out of China’s compute market would enable the country to develop its own AI chips to challenge Nvidia internationally.
China is already moving in that direction. Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China. Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024. At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
Still, the allegations involving Alice Huang open new scrutiny of the company’s business relationships and could taint any assurances Nvidia offers that it can prevent sensitive technology from reaching unauthorized customers.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly warned officials close to Trump earlier this year about Huang’s relationship with an alleged spy. Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: The two East German officials who accidentally brought down the Berlin Wall
articles.title_zh: The two East German officials who accidentally brought down the Berlin Wall
articles.content_orig:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called for the protection of freedom and democracy in Germany and Europe on the 37th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall.
In a post on Monday on X, Merz recalled the three pivotal events of November 9 in German history: the proclamation of the republic in 1918, the Nazi pogroms of 1938 against Jews, and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.
"November 9 stands for the darkest and happiest hours of our history: for anti-Semitism and persecution, for the beginning of democracy and the fall of the wall," Merz said.
Merz added: "Freedom and democracy are never a given. Let us protect them - in Germany and Europe."
November 9 holds a unique place in Germany's collective memory.
In 1918, the abdication of Kaiser Wilhelm II paved the way for the proclamation of the republic; in 1938, the Nazi regime unleashed nationwide attacks that marked the start of the systematic killing of Jews and a sharp increase in their persecution; and in 1989, the fall of the Berlin Wall signalled the end of Germany's division and the start of reunification.
Later on Monday, Merz will attend a ceremony in Munich marking the 20th anniversary of the establishment of the Ohel Jakob synagogue, alongside Bavarian premier Markus Söder and the president of the Bavarian state parliament, Ilse Aigner.
Aigner is widely expected to be nominated to succeed outgoing federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, potentially becoming the first woman to serve as German president.

articles.title_orig: Trump talked with Fed chief, but there’s no record of it on Warsh’s calendar
articles.title_zh: Trump talked with Fed chief, but there’s no record of it on Warsh’s calendar
articles.content_orig:
Tom Boggioni is a writer, born, raised and living in San Diego — where he attended San Diego State University. Prior to writing for Raw Story, he wrote for FireDogLake, blogged as TBogg, and worked in banking, marketing and construction.
Democrats want answers from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh , demanding to know whether he is hiding secret conversations with Donald Trump .
The president says he and Warsh have talked. Warsh’s official records say they haven’t. And the Fed chair isn’t explaining the gap, the Washington Post reported.
On Friday, the Fed released Warsh’s September calendar, and once again, Trump’s name doesn’t appear. That makes "five months in a row," every month since Warsh took over in May, with no logged contact with the president. It comes despite a request this summer from Senate Democrats that he include any such conversations.
According to the Post, " The calendars are one of the few windows into how often a president reaches the official who leads the central bank’s decisions on interest rates , and previous Fed chairs have recorded interactions with presidents there. The Fed is designed to operate independently of the White House , setting rates based on its own best assessment of the economy rather than short-term political pressure."
On Sept. 16, the same day Warsh and his colleagues raised rates a quarter point against Trump’s wishes, the president told reporters he had weighed in on Warsh’s vote.
“I talked to Kevin, and I said, ‘You might as well vote with the board ’cause it’s not gonna matter,’” Trump said, noting that Warsh lacked the votes to change the outcome.
When a reporter asked if he had tried to sway Warsh, Trump said he hadn’t. “No, I didn’t convince him. No, I said, ‘Do what you want,’” he said, adding that he wanted Warsh “to be independent.”
Neither side has cleared it up, the report notes. The White House has refused to say when that conversation took place, and Warsh won’t confirm it ever happened.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) and three other Democratic senators wrote to Warsh in August, asking him to state in writing whether he had spoken with Trump and to correct his calendars if so. Van Hollen’s office told the Post on Friday that Warsh never replied.
“It’s clear neither Warsh nor Trump give a damn about transparency to the American people,” Van Hollen said. “Under a Democratic majority in Congress, we will continue pushing for that much-needed transparency.”

articles.title_zh: US-led peace talks for Russia and Ukraine will look at security guarantees for both sides
articles.content_orig:
US secretary of state says some progress made on what security infrastructure could look like in Ukraine and Europe after the war. What we know on day 1,720
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said some progress had been made on what the “security infrastructure” of Ukraine and Europe could look like after the war with Russia, adding that talks this week could lead to further advances. Rubio’s comments on Sunday, ahead of his travel to Paris for talks with G7 foreign ministers, come as Russia-Ukraine negotiations under US mediation have been set for Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump’s son-in-law, will represent the US in Abu Dhabi.
In an interview ‌with CBS’s “60 Minutes” broadcast on Sunday, Trump said he believed the war would end ‌soon and suggested Ukraine could emerge from a settlement with altered borders. “I think we’re gonna have it done, and I think it’s gonna happen and they’re gonna end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine,” Trump said. Asked whether Russian president Vladimir Putin was stringing him along, Trump replied: “Oh, I don’t think so.”
On Sunday, Rubio said the whole time the US had been talking about Russia and Ukraine, “the one thing that’s repeatedly come up is the need for security guarantees” and what they would look like in Ukraine, and on the European continent. “I think that’s what the president’s alluding to – is that there’s been some advances made in what that architecture could look like post-conflict.”
French ⁠Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Europe would be well represented at the talks. “France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in ⁠these discussions,” Barrot told French radio station RTL. “I can’t ​tell you yet who will be ‌representing France on this ‌occasion, but France will certainly be there,” he added.
A Russian drone has struck emergency workers on rescue missions in southern Ukraine. Authorities say the attack on Sunday hit a former school and nearby shelter in the village of Komyshuvakha, previously targeted by Russian bombs. Ukraine said last Monday’s attack killed at least 55 people. No injuries were reported in Sunday’s strike but rescue equipment was damaged. About 50 people remain missing.
Power has been restored to the Russian-controlled ⁠Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine, hours after the plant lost its external electricity ⁠supply and had ⁠to ​use backup generators for reactor cooling, the UN’s nuclear watchdog said on Sunday. Zaporizhzhia, which does ⁠not produce electricity but needs power supplied by two external links to keep nuclear fuel cool, lost ⁠its off-site electricity supply earlier on Sunday after the Ferosplavna power ​line disconnected. The International Atomic ‌Energy Agency said the cause and location of the disconnection were unknown. The loss of power was the plant’s 27th such incident since the beginning of the conflict.
Russia said ⁠on Sunday overnight strikes by its forces had hit three cargo vessels ⁠that were carrying military ⁠goods ​for Ukraine and two electricity substations , which it said supplied power to ⁠the Ukrainian defence industry, Reuters reports. Russia’s defence ministry said Russian forces had struck a container ship delivering ⁠weapons and military equipment to the Black Sea ​port of Odesa, ‌and another in ‌the port of Chornomorsk, which is in the same ‌southwestern region of Ukraine. According to the ministry, the second container ship had delivered dual-use cargo to Ukraine. It said a third vessel, a dry cargo ship hit south-west of Odesa, ‌was carrying weapons and military equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces.
Moldova on Sunday launched a new power line connecting the country to neighbouring Romania and the European grid, to reduce its reliance on Russian energy . “For decades, Moscow used energy to blackmail us,” President Maia Sandu wrote on X. “No more. Moldova buys zero Russian gas.” Achieving energy security is a priority for the former Soviet republic of 2.6 million people, which has faced difficulties since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title_orig: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.title_zh: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.content_orig:
France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions "at the European level".
Iran is yet to respond to Barrot's allegations.
The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across several other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
Separately on Monday, the Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed but the Iranian regime.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
And in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction spoiling food. The incidents are also being investigated as deliberate cyber attacks, Reuters reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.

articles.title_orig: Israeli opposition eyes deal with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties to oust Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Israeli opposition eyes deal with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties to oust Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Avigdor Liberman's 2018 haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription proposal has reemerged as a potential basis for coalition negotiations after the Yisrael Beytenu chairman signaled on Sunday that he was willing to compromise with ultra-Orthodox parties. But how does the proposal compare with the draft legislation promoted by Boaz Bismuth in 2025, and would either framework meet the IDF's growing manpower needs?
The 2018 proposal, developed by the Defense Ministry and the IDF during Liberman's tenure as defense minister, sought to gradually increase haredi enlistment while preserving military service deferrals for yeshiva students. It established annual recruitment targets, financial penalties for institutions that failed to meet them, and a mechanism that could ultimately terminate the special exemption arrangement if recruitment targets were repeatedly missed.
Unlike Bismuth's proposal, which introduced additional personal sanctions against individual yeshiva students, Liberman's framework primarily targeted yeshiva funding and the continued validity of the exemption system itself. It also set a lower exemption age of 24, compared with 26 under Bismuth's proposal.
The differences have taken on renewed political significance as Gadi Eisenkot prepares to receive the mandate to form a government. Liberman's decision to lift his veto on cooperation with haredi parties has opened the door to coalition negotiations, although he maintains that his willingness to compromise does not amount to abandoning his support for universal conscription.
"Willingness to compromise does not mean abandoning values and principles," Liberman wrote in a statement on Sunday, defending his change in political position amid criticism from commentators and journalists.
He emphasized that his 2018 proposal would require adjustments in light of the October 7 attacks and the subsequent increase in the military's manpower requirements.
"It is clear to me that following the events of October 7, the law I proposed in 2018 also requires changes and adjustments, but it still constitutes a suitable basis for reaching agreements," he wrote.
Liberman's 2018 legislation was developed by a committee comprising representatives of the Defense Ministry and the IDF. It passed its first reading in the Knesset in July of that year.
The proposal aimed to increase military enlistment among ultra-Orthodox men without dismantling the existing yeshiva system. It allowed many students to continue deferring their service while establishing gradually increasing recruitment targets.
Bismuth's 2025 proposal similarly preserved the possibility of service deferrals and exemptions but added personal restrictions intended to encourage enlistment.
Neither proposal established an immediate and equal military conscription requirement for all young haredi men.
One of the most significant differences between the proposals concerned the age at which yeshiva students could receive exemptions from military service. Liberman's framework set the exemption age at 24, while Bismuth's proposed legislation raised it to 26.
The enforcement mechanisms also differed substantially.
Under Liberman's framework, annual recruitment targets were accompanied by financial sanctions against yeshivas if those targets were not met.
The proposal's most consequential provision addressed prolonged failures to meet recruitment quotas. If actual enlistment remained below 85% of the annual target for three consecutive years, the amendment to the law would expire after an additional 12 months.
This meant that the special arrangement allowing military service deferrals and exemptions could not continue indefinitely if recruitment targets were repeatedly missed.
However, Liberman's proposal did not establish a new system of personal sanctions against individual yeshiva students who failed to enlist.
Instead, its enforcement mechanisms focused primarily on financial penalties for religious institutions and the continued validity of the exemption system.
The committee that developed the framework also recommended expanding administrative sanctions against deserters and draft evaders.
Bismuth's proposal, by contrast, introduced personal sanctions alongside financial penalties for yeshivas that failed to comply with the law.
Those proposed restrictions included limitations on overseas travel, obtaining a new driver's license before age 23, and eligibility for certain government benefits and economic incentives.
However, the personal sanctions were not all designed to take effect automatically or immediately.
Some depended on the issuance of an enlistment order and the individual's subsequent failure to report for duty. Others were linked to failures to meet broader recruitment targets, while certain restrictions were subject to age limits or delayed implementation dates.
The proposal also included provisions allowing sanctions to be eased or exemptions to be granted under specified circumstances.
For individual yeshiva students, Bismuth's framework was therefore more stringent because it introduced additional personal restrictions.
On the exemption system as a whole, however, Liberman's proposal established a potentially more far-reaching consequence for persistent failures to meet recruitment targets.
Under his framework, the special legislative arrangement could expire following three consecutive years of missed targets, subject to the stipulated 12-month transition period.
Bismuth's proposal included review mechanisms, financial sanctions, and possible adjustments, but did not establish an equivalent automatic mechanism terminating the entire exemption arrangement.
The differences are also evident in the recruitment targets themselves.
Liberman's framework established a target of 3,996 recruits in 2018, gradually increasing to 4,967 in 2021 and 6,208 in 2025.
One version of Bismuth's framework set a target of 8,160 recruits over 18 months, averaging about 5,440 per year.
Under that version, up to 10% of the recruitment target could be met by individuals performing civilian service in security-related fields.
At first glance, Bismuth's initial target appears higher than the target Liberman established for 2018. However, Bismuth's annual average was lower than the target Liberman's proposal established for 2025.
The figures do not represent identical periods or legislative arrangements operating under equivalent timetables.
Several versions of the recruitment targets were presented during the advancement of Bismuth's framework. Each figure must therefore be examined in light of the specific legislative version and period it refers to.
Another significant difference concerns how recruits are counted.
Liberman's framework established targets for national and civilian service separately from military enlistment targets.
Under one version of Bismuth's proposal, civilian service in security-related fields could count toward the overall recruitment quota, up to 10% of the target.
Consequently, meeting the overall quota would not necessarily indicate that an equivalent number of new soldiers had joined the IDF.
The identity of those included in the recruitment figures has also sparked controversy.
One criticism of Bismuth's framework concerned the possibility of counting young men who had already left the haredi community.
If a young man raised in the ultra-Orthodox community but no longer studying at a yeshiva is counted as a haredi recruit, meeting the recruitment target does not necessarily demonstrate increased enlistment among students attending active yeshivas.
Beyond these legal and numerical differences lies a fundamental change in Israel's security requirements.
Liberman's proposal was developed in 2018, five years before the October 7 attacks and the war that followed.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s tech allies face a revolt from within their own industry
articles.title_zh: Trump’s tech allies face a revolt from within their own industry
articles.content_orig:
Democrats won seats on anti-datacentre tickets and Musk wasted nearly half a billion dollars. Big tech may be losing its grip, but it won’t go quietly
P hotos That Precede Unfortunate Events: a couple of months back, Donald Trump hosted some of the world’s most powerful tech executives at the White House for a “ Super Intelligence luncheon ”, which by coincidence is also how my mum described her tuna sandwiches in a forlorn attempt to get me to eat them. Sitting either side of the president were Elon Musk, making a rare offline appearance in daylight hours, and Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief executive carving out a precious slot in what we now know was an extremely busy schedule.
Over a delicious meal of microchips and rare-earth metals, the billionaires sketched out a utopian future of an AI industry unencumbered by regulation or safeguards, powered by their heroic strongman leader, a political genius effortlessly able to impose his will upon an entire nation. And perhaps it should have been apparent even at the time that these (mostly) men were putting their faith in a guy who had recently been defeated by pond algae . But as the drinks and the good times flowed, it was still possible to believe that the sun would never set on the thousand-year American superintelligence empire.
And so, while we’re all learning lessons from the resounding defeat delivered to Trumpism last week, might we start with a modest and sober reassessment of the Silicon Valley oligarch class? For years, we have been told that these are some of humanity’s greatest seers and visionaries, the Leonardos and Einsteins of the 21st century, the people best placed to plot a course for our species, despite for the most part not being able to smile without looking as though they were undergoing a juice enema.
As it turned out, this small band of brilliant clairvoyants somehow failed to anticipate the possibility that the deeply unpopular man they were clasping in a tender embrace would be subjected to an absolute democracy-mogging in just a few weeks, throwing their altruistic wet dreams into chaos. After all, last week’s midterms were not simply a rebuke to one man or one party, but to an entire ideology. Across the US, voters took their revenge not just on big tech, but on the politicians who had enabled it.
In Texas, Gina Hinojosa beat the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott, by promising an immediate moratorium on datacentre development, and despite being outspent almost eight to one, in large part by big tech donors desperate to preserve their tax breaks. In Ohio, the Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown described his opponent, Jon Husted, as “the face of datacentres”, a visually horrifying concept. In total, 46 of the 47 ballot measures relating to datacentres were defeated . By Thursday morning, the markets had responded with a devastating sell-off of tech stocks , the repercussions of which are still shaking out as you read this.
Should we read anything into the fact that the biggest progressive landslide in 52 years, catalysed by a concerted mobilisation of Black, Latino and young voters, was sufficient to send the financial markets into existential panic? Anyone able to join the dots for us there? Is it relevant that the São Paulo stock exchange plunged about 14% after Lula da Silva’s shock election victory in Brazil last month? Just what is it about the popular repudiation of hard-right autocrats that appears to spook the pillars of capitalism so much?
For the time being, big tech does not appear to be as politically polarising in Britain as it is in the US. This is largely because much of the recent acceleration has occurred under a Labour administration, in particular under the late lamented Keir Starmer, a prime minister who in retrospect may actually have been a semi-sentient chatbot all along. “We will test and understand AI before we regulate it,” Starmer once said, which he appears to have done by plugging it directly into his own mouth for two years. But this is an issue that will continue to rise in democratic salience, in part because it relies on the undemocratic manufacture of consent, an inexorable march deliberately designed to circumvent scrutiny.
after newsletter promotion
Take the UK government’s AI growth zones , designed to supercharge datacentre development by taking decisions on nationally significant infrastructure projects (NSIP) away from local councils. A recent report by Spotlight on Corruption found that over two years, ministers met only two community groups and no environmental organisations while developing the policy, while at the same time ministers and senior civil servants were hired to 38 roles at AI companies. Naturally, you are likely to hear very little opposition to any of this, either from the billionaire-owned press or the official opposition; indeed, Kemi Badenoch is perhaps the only major party leader you can imagine typing “what do I think of AI” into an AI prompt.
You will occasionally hear the assumption, made on both sides of the Atlantic and often on the flimsiest of evidence, that voters are increasingly fed up with democracy. But what if we’re getting this the wrong way round? What if, in fact, it is those who are supposed to be upholding democracy – the politicians and media and captains of industry, all slowly stewing in X-brained algorithmic talking points – who are beginning to tire of it? While Musk spends enormous chunks of his fortune trying (and failing) to tip the electoral scales in favour of the hard right, Reform UK rakes in £72m in donations from two cryptocurrency billionaires. Bonus question: do we think the brave men and women out there on the tech frontier will respond to democratic setbacks by demanding more democratic accountability, or less?
And, of course, in these febrile and fragile times you have to take your wins wherever you get them. But as any ChatGPT user will tell you, making bold claims on the basis of a bare minimum of data is always an exercise fraught with risk. Saying no once will never be enough. In a note to investors last week, Goldman Sachs wrote: “We expect the datacentre issue to somewhat fade in importance and any moratoria on datacentre development to be short-lived.” You can decide for yourself what it means by that.
Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist

articles.title_orig: Carney Recruits Bridgewater Co-CIO to Run Canada Sovereign Wealth Fund
articles.title_zh: Carney Recruits Bridgewater Co-CIO to Run Canada Sovereign Wealth Fund
articles.content_orig:
Karen Karniol-Tambour at the Milken Institute Global Conference in Beverly Hills in 2023. Ms. Karniol-Tambour will lead the Canada Strong Fund, which Prime Minister Mark Carney has described as a sovereign wealth fund. MIKE BLAKE/Reuters
Karen Karniol-Tambour, the co-chief investment officer at U.S.-based hedge fund manager Bridgewater Associates, has been named as the first CEO of the Canada Strong Fund.
Prime Minister Mark Carney made the announcement Monday in a news release.
“The Canada Strong Fund will put Canadian capital to work in the projects and companies building our country’s future. Ms. Karniol-Tambour brings the experience and ambition to lead this mission – making investments that strengthen our economy and build lasting wealth for Canadians. As we build a stronger, more independent Canada, we are ensuring Canadians have a direct stake in its success,” Mr. Carney said in a statement.
Mr. Carney first announced the fund in April, which he described as Canada’s first national sovereign wealth fund. The fund has not yet launched.
It will have an initial capital commitment of $25-billion.
The government said it will invest on commercial terms through two main streams: co-investments in national-building projects, as well as “strategic investments in other high-potential projects and companies” to secure long-term returns.
Ms. Karniol-Tambour is a Canadian citizen who joined Bridgewater in 2006. She has been the company’s co-CIO since 2023.
According to a biography published on the Prime Minister’s website, the co-CIO position involves overseeing the development investment models and client portfolios, including those focused on Asia.

France on Monday said Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were behind “unprecedented” cyberattacks on supermarket fridges in the country last month, vowing sanctions on a European level against Tehran.
That would make the hacks among the most disruptive cyberattacks of the war with Iran that began in February, a conflict that has been marked by scattered incidents of alleged cyber disruption. articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
LONDON, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Brent crude futures were down almost 5% on Monday after hitting their lowest since early September, after US President Donald Trump downplayed the likelihood of renewed strikes on Iran, though attacks continued on ships near the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude futures ‌were down $4.57, or 4.65%, at $93.75 a barrel by 12:04 p.m. EDT (1704 GMT). Their session low was $92.80 a barrel.
US West Texas Intermediate futures fell $3.19, or 3.51%, ‌to $87.64.
The Brent benchmark plunged by 16% last week and touched a two-month low of $93.22, its steepest weekly drop since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.
On Sunday, Trump said he was highly unlikely to order fresh ​attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progressed. Still, both countries reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz.
"This seems to have encouraged sellers on the prospects for peace even while the actual fighting is not slowing down," TACenergy analysts said in a note.
Last week, Trump had hinted at a resumption of attacks on Iran, and Tehran vowed to respond by striking US and Israeli targets. But there has been no sign of a large-scale US military operation.
A senior Iranian security ‌official told the country's state media that Tehran has no ⁠plans to negotiate unless Washington takes practical steps to meet seven conditions set out in a June interim agreement.
Saudi Arabia's foreign minister and his Omani counterpart stressed in a phone call on Monday the need to press ahead with diplomatic efforts to contain the ⁠regional crisis and safeguard maritime security and sea lanes, Saudi state media reported.
On Monday, Trump will meet the prime minister of Qatar, which has been a mediator, though senior US and Gulf officials cast doubt on the chances of an imminent deal.
Iraq has reached understandings with the US to allow Iraqi oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz via a shipping lane near ​Oman, ​Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said in an interview with Al Jazeera on Sunday.
"Crude futures are under ​selling pressure once again as oil volumes continue strong through the ‌Strait of Hormuz", said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at BOK Financial.
In the Medina region, a fire was extinguished after Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline was struck, an Energy Ministry source said, according to state media. There were no casualties and the pipeline's operations were not affected.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for an attack on Sunday at Saudi oil giant Aramco's corporate office in the heart of the financial district of the capital Riyadh. Debris from the attempted attack blew out windows across several floors, the Saudi energy ministry said.
"Fresh tanker incidents and an attack on Saudi Aramco's offices show that shipping and regional security risks remain unresolved as traders price in a less ‌disruptive outcome," said Gelber & Associates.
WELL-SUPPLIED PHYSICAL MARKET
Dated Brent, used to price cargoes around the world, has ​weakened to a discount to the nearby Brent futures contract, Morgan Stanley said in a report on ​Monday, highlighting weakness in the physical market.
The global oil market is showing signs ​of a return to excess supply as demand drops because of high prices, some analysts said. The global oil surplus is estimated ‌at around 1.4 million bpd in October, JP Morgan said in a ​report last week.
OPEC oil output rose in ​October, a Reuters survey found, led by gains in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq despite continued constraints on exports.
Crude output by the 11-member Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries rose by 1.38 million barrels per day from the previous month to 22.87 million bpd, the survey found.
US crude oil and product stockpiles ​were expected to have fallen last week, a preliminary Reuters ‌poll showed on Monday.
Stocks of crude oil in the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to 279.5 million barrels last week, the lowest level since ​October 1982, according to data from the Department of Energy.

articles.title_orig: No deal on Ukraine aid? Then no deal on EU budget, Merz says
articles.title_zh: No deal on Ukraine aid? Then no deal on EU budget, Merz says
articles.content_orig:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has made the deal on the European Union's next budget conditional on fresh support for Ukraine, bringing together two politically sensitive topics that have exposed deep divisions among member states.
Kyiv is staring down a €70 billion shortfall in its 2027 budget caused by Russia's relentless airstrikes. The EU has promised to cover two-thirds of this gap, roughly €45 billion, through a yet-to-be-defined instrument.
"A collective commitment that all of us, without exception, will contribute fairly to closing this gap is an essential prerequisite for resolving this issue and for discussing any further matters, particularly those with financial implications," Merz said in a letter addressed to European Council President António Costa and seen by Euronews.
Merz argued that the ongoing negotiations on the bloc's seven-year budget should guarantee "a solution supported by all member states that ensures a sound and multiannual financing perspective for Ukraine from 2028 onwards, including the interest liabilities that have already accrued".
The interest refers to the ongoing €90 billion support loan, which is backed by common borrowing among 24 countries. Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic secured an opt-out from the credit line in exchange for providing the necessary unanimity.
The principal will not be repaid until Russia agrees to war reparations. However, interest payments will start falling due next year. Initially, Brussels estimated €3 billion per year, but the steep rise in borrowing costs has altered the calculation.
The €45 billion that the EU intends to provide Kyiv in 2027 will come on top of the existing loan.
Given the massive scale of the gap, a new round of joint debt has quickly emerged as the frontrunner option. The European Commission is set to present countries with possible options ahead of a special summit at the end of the month.
In the letter, Merz asks Costa to accelerate the timeline for discussions by putting the matter as a "priority" at this week's informal summit in Dublin. The topic was not originally foreseen in the agenda.
The chancellor pointedly regrets that financial and military support for the war-weary country is "distributed unevenly and carried mostly by only a few member states".
"Supporting Ukraine is a matter of our indivisible European security, and so must be the burden sharing for that support," he writes.
Germany is the largest bilateral donor to Ukraine. Other key backers, such as Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden, share Merz's grievances and want to merge the budget and Ukraine into one single package.
All these countries happen to belong to the so-called "frugals" or "modernisers" who advocate across-the-board cuts to the draft budget. This has put them on a collision course with the "Friends of Cohesion", who are fighting to retain a high level of expenditure.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia are signalling they will once again exempt themselves from joint debt to support Kyiv. Bulgaria, a vocal critic of weapons deliveries, is expected to follow suit. The four sit in the cohesion group.
Their refusal to participate has angered the so-called “frugal” countries.
"The cohesion camp cannot have their cake and eat it," a diplomat said. "There is no money tree in Brussels, so we need to make political choices."
Simon Harris, Ireland's finance minister, whose country holds the rotating presidency and moderates negotiations, sided with the "frugals".
"It's very hard to have a serious conversation about the European budget for the next several years without Ukraine and the financing of Ukraine," Harris said on Monday morning before heading into a ministerial meeting in Brussels.
"We do need to frame this correctly. This is actually European security."
But not all member states share the same position.
Ignacy Niemczycki, Poland's deputy minister in charge of European affairs, argued last week that the two issues are fundamentally distinct and binding them together could "backfire" and make a final deal "even more difficult" than it is now.
Meanwhile, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico warned that such a link would be "very dangerous".

The Japan-only model arrives on December 10th in a midnight black color scheme.
Sony is launching a new version of its PlayStation Portal exclusively in Japan next month. The updated model will launch in the midnight black color option we’ve seen before , and will include “additional” internal storage for future-looking features.
It’s the additional internal storage that’s the surprise change to this particular model, which will be locked to Japanese language options and can only be used with a PlayStation account registered in Japan. Sony says the extra storage is for “future functionality” that it will announce once these features are finalized.
Sony is also renaming this particular Portal from PlayStation Portal Remote Player to PlayStation Portal Player. The name change, combined with extra internal storage, seems to suggest that this particular model might get access to streaming apps.
The existing PlayStation Portal doesn’t support streaming apps like YouTube, Disney Plus, or Netflix, and is primarily designed to stream PS5 games from a console or the cloud. The PlayStation Portal isn’t powerful enough to play PlayStation games locally, but extra storage could also let you sync media for offline playback.
This Japan-only PlayStation Portal is launching on December 10th, priced at 39,980 yen (around $253).

articles.title_orig: Palestinian Authority land freeze targets Arab Israelis after Jewish home purchases near Jericho
articles.title_zh: Palestinian Authority land freeze targets Arab Israelis after Jewish home purchases near Jericho
articles.content_orig:
The Palestinian Authority temporarily suspended land registration transactions last week for people holding Israeli citizenship or Jerusalem residency, following the purchase of eight homes by Jewish activists near Jericho, a city in Area A, according to an official announcement by the Palestinian Land Authority.
Lt.-Col. (res.) Maurice Hirsch, director of the Initiative for Palestinian Authority Accountability and Reform at the Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs, argued that the PA likely believed the Israeli Jews had acquired the homes with the assistance of Israeli Arabs.
Palestinian law treats the sale or lease of land to Israeli Jews as an act of treason, which can carry severe penalties, including life imprisonment with hard labor and potentially the death penalty. In 2019, a Nablus court sentenced a Palestinian man to five years in prison for allegedly attempting to sell land to Israeli Jews. In 2018, a Kalkilya court sentenced two Palestinian men to 15 years of hard labor for their involvement in a network seeking to transfer West Bank land to Israeli Jews.
“The decision exposes a fundamental contradiction in Palestinian Authority policy. While the PA considers Arab citizens and residents of Israel to be Palestinians, it now treats their Israeli citizenship as grounds for restricting their property transactions,” Hirsch wrote in a publication for the JCPA.
He added: “The PA’s latest restrictions on Israeli Arab property transactions represent another dimension of this policy, extending its consequences beyond Palestinians living under PA jurisdiction to Arab citizens and residents of Israel.”
The PA has long regarded the approximately two million Arab citizens of Israel as Palestinian, regardless of their integration into Israeli society, military service, or self-described identities. However, the latest suspension, though a temporary restriction that has now been lifted, introduced one of the first distinctions based on the Israeli citizenship and residency status of Arabs.
Despite the Oslo Accords excluding Israeli citizens from the PA’s personal jurisdiction, the PA has attempted to prosecute Israeli Arabs in the past for their alleged roles in land transfers to Jews and other alleged crimes.
The location of the eight homes is also significant. Although Jericho is in Area A, under PA civil and security control, the properties in question are located in Area C, which is under full Israeli civil and security control. Under the Oslo Accords, the PA’s territorial jurisdiction does not extend to Area C, and Israeli citizens are also excluded from its personal jurisdiction. This raises questions about the PA’s authority to investigate or prosecute Israeli citizens in connection with the purchases, even if Israeli Arabs were involved in facilitating the transactions.

articles.title_orig: Honda to invest $3 billion in new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio
articles.title_zh: Honda to invest $3 billion in new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio
articles.content_orig:
MARYSVILLE, Ohio — Honda Motor plans to invest $3 billion to build a new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio, the automaker announced Monday.
Honda said the new plant, which will be near its other facilities in Marysville, Ohio, is expected to begin production in 2029, have a capacity for 240,000 vehicles annually and create more than 2,000 jobs.
The facility is expected to be capable of producing traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines, all-electric vehicles and hybrid models, which have been growing in popularity in the U.S.
The plant is expected to increase Honda's light-duty vehicle capacity to 1.3 million units annually in the U.S. It currently has 12 manufacturing plants in United States, eight of which produce engines or light-duty vehicles for the auto industry.
It's the company's first new mass production U.S. vehicle assembly plant since it opened a facility in Indiana in 2008. It also opened a $70 million performance vehicle facility in 2016 and a multibillion-dollar joint venture battery plant earlier this year, both in Ohio.
"This is not simply an investment in another plant. It is an investment in the future of Honda manufacturing in America," Bob Nelson, executive vice president of American Honda Motor, said during the announcement at the company's U.S. heritage center in Ohio.
The auto industry has been trying to localize more production amid President Donald Trump 's tariffs and inflated logistics costs that have cut into profits.
Honda's plans for a new plant come roughly two weeks after Volkswagen-owned luxury brand Audi announced it would invest more than $4 billion in its first U.S. manufacturing facility in Georgia.
Detroit automakers General Motors and Ford Motor and international automakers Toyota Motor and Hyundai Motor also recently said they will spend billions of dollars on new or updated U.S. facilities.
Honda's announcement comes after the automaker in May indefinitely suspended an $11 billion investment plan to produce all-electric vehicles and batteries in Canada. It also canceled three planned EVs for the U.S. market.
The new Ohio plant is expected to notably boost Honda's U.S. production and American-produced sales. Honda said nearly all of its vehicles sold in the U.S., including its Acura luxury brand, were produced in North America, including more than 60% in the U.S.
American Honda Motor Co. executive Jennifer Thomas recently emphasized the Japanese automaker's commitment to the U.S. and need for additional capacity.
"In order to be competitive in this market, you're going to need to build products here," Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs, said Oct. 27 in Detroit. "We are focused on trying to maximize the existing capacity that we have, but we are at capacity, and so we're exploring all options."
Thomas also warned the automotive industry faces a "catastrophic" scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, when Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don't reach a deal.
Honda said it has built more than 33 million vehicles and more than 39 million engines in the U.S. since it started auto production in the U.S. in 1982.
The Japanese automaker currently has more than 30,000 employees in the U.S.

articles.title_orig: Syria Signs Deal With China for 6.5 Million Prepaid Electricity Meters, Raising Questions Over Consumer Costs
articles.title_zh: Syria Signs Deal With China for 6.5 Million Prepaid Electricity Meters, Raising Questions Over Consumer Costs
articles.content_orig:
[DAMASCUS] The Syrian Electricity Company signed an agreement with Chinese company Wasion Group Limited on Sunday to supply 6.5 million prepaid smart electricity meters, as part of efforts to modernize electricity consumption monitoring and improve power grid management in Syria. The deal raises questions about its cost, financing arrangements, and potential impact on consumers’ electricity bills.
The agreement was signed at the Syrian Electricity Company’s headquarters in Damascus, in the presence of representatives from both the Syrian and Chinese sides, as part of a broader government plan to modernize the energy sector and introduce digital systems into electricity services.
The media office of the Syrian Electricity Company, which operates under the Ministry of Energy, told The Media Line that the agreement includes the supply of 6 million single-phase meters, primarily intended for residential properties and small businesses, along with 500,000 three-phase meters, typically used by commercial and industrial facilities requiring greater electrical capacity.
According to the media office, the agreement also includes software systems and technical equipment necessary to operate the meters, allowing for more accurate consumption measurements, improved customer data management, reduced electricity losses, and more efficient network monitoring.
The media office explained that the prepaid metering system requires consumers to purchase electricity credit before using power, rather than paying periodic bills based on consumption recorded after use.
The new system is expected to improve electricity bill collection, reduce errors associated with traditional meter readings, and enable subscribers to monitor their electricity consumption more accurately.

The official announcement did not disclose the financial value of the contract or specify who would bear the costs of purchasing and installing the meters. It also did not clarify whether subscribers would be required to pay fees to replace their existing meters or how the prepaid system would be implemented for low-income households.
Authorities have also not announced a specific timetable for delivering all the meters covered by the agreement or identified which governorates will be included in the initial phase of implementation.
Khaled Abu Di, director of the General Establishment for Electricity Transmission and Distribution, previously announced that the institution had developed a plan to replace conventional electricity meters with smart meters over approximately three years.
In January 2026, Abu Di revealed that around 1.2 million electricity subscribers in Syria still lacked electricity meters, highlighting the scale of the challenges involved in modernizing metering, billing, and revenue collection systems.
The agreement comes as Syria’s electricity sector continues to face significant challenges following years of war, including damage to power generation facilities and transmission and distribution networks, as well as the need for substantial investment to rehabilitate infrastructure and improve the reliability of electricity supplies.
Although introducing smart meters could improve consumption management and reduce commercial electricity losses, modernizing metering systems does not necessarily mean an increase in electricity generation or an end to power outages. Improving the number of hours electricity is available also requires upgrading power plants, transmission and distribution networks, and securing reliable energy supplies.
The prepaid nature of the new meters raises additional questions about their impact on Syrian households, particularly amid difficult economic conditions and concerns about consumers’ ability to regularly purchase electricity credit.
It also remains unclear whether the government intends to introduce changes to electricity tariffs alongside the new system or will limit the initiative to modernizing metering and payment collection procedures.
The agreement represents another step in economic and technological cooperation between Syria and China, as Damascus seeks to attract foreign companies to participate in rehabilitating public services and infrastructure.

articles.title_zh: Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention
articles.content_orig:
An inquiry from the U.S. Commerce Dept. into Singapore data center Megaspeed was transferred to the Department of Justice after Nvidia NVDA intervened, The New York Times reported.
Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter reached out for information to the Commerce Dept., according to the news outlet. Teter did so after Nvidia received permission from Jeff Kessler, a top official at the Commerce Department. Kessler reports directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
The inquiry into Megaspeed was then transferred to the DOJ to avoid a potential compromise into the investigation, the news outlet added, citing people familiar with the matter. The DOJ is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed, people familiar with the matter told the news outlet.
The Commerce Dept. did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Seeking Alpha.
Over the weekend, Nvidia's board of directors disclosed that it opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang on the prospect of potentially being targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. Separately, Huang disclosed that he had been unfaithful to his wife in conjunction with the matter with Alice Huang (no relation), a Singapore-based data center executive.
Ms. Huang, who also goes by Huang Le, is alleged to have spied on the Nvidia founder. U.S. officials have been investigating Huang and Megaspeed since 2024.
Nvidia shares fell 4.5% in late morning trading amid investor scrutiny following the disclosure.
A number of Wall Street firms weighed in on the matter, including Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives, one of Nvidia's biggest bulls on Wall Street.
“Jensen has become the global face of the AI Revolution and that now will be front and center for Nvidia how to navigate this very difficult situation looking forward,” Ives wrote in a note to clients. “This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons.” Disclaimer Content provided by Seeking Alpha is intended for information purposes only, and that Seeking Alpha does not offer any personalist investment advice and is not a licensed securities dealer, broker, US investment adviser or investment bank.

articles.title_orig: Stocks Climb as Buyers Step In Despite Nvidia Woes: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks Climb as Buyers Step In Despite Nvidia Woes: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Stocks surged on Monday, boosted by a decline in oil prices as well as gains in technology shares after last week's volatility.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average popped 1,113 points, or 2.2%, supported by gains in stocks such as Goldman Sachs and Caterpillar . The S&P 500 rose 2.3%, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 2.5%.
With Monday's rally, the Dow is now above the level it closed on Election Day. The S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq still remain slightly below, however.
Oil prices fell on Monday, lifting investor sentiment. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures dropped 3% to around $87 per barrel. International benchmark Brent slid 4% to about $94 per barrel.
Friday's market partially rebounded from Thursday's brutal AI-driven sell-off, as chip stocks recovered on renewed buying. However, concerns linger in the wake of the Democrats' strong midterm results, with investors fearing that tighter regulations on data center construction, energy use, and development costs could slow the AI infrastructure boom .
The tech sector also focused on the bombshell announcement Sunday that Nvidia's board of directors is opening an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares were last down 6%.
"Magnificent Seven" names were higher contrary to Nvidia. Amazon gained 3%, while Tesla and Alphabet climbed 5% and 2%, respectively. Microsoft also added 2%.
Other chip stocks advanced as well, with Broadcom popping 8% and Advanced Micro Devices jumping 12%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) — which dropped around 13% last week — rose more than 6%.
The recent chip sell-off was "overdone," said Jay Hatfield, CEO at Infrastructure Capital Advisors. The turmoil was still "partially correct," he added, given that there "definitely is a policy overhang from the Democrats in both the short run, but, more importantly, in the long run from '28." To be sure, he believes data centers are ultimately "going to get built" in the U.S.
For the broader market, Hatfield said that "it's not like the coast is clear" with Monday's bounce. In fact, he anticipates the S&P 500 will be rangebound through the end of the year.
"There are still a lot of overhangs on the market," the CEO said, pointing to elevated oil prices as a result of the Middle East conflict as well as the Federal Reserve's interest rate outlook.
This week , investors are looking ahead to key AI-related earnings — CoreWeave , Cisco and Applied Materials are all on deck — as they assess the outlook for tech and whether the recent selloff has further to run.
They'll also watch for the releases of both the consumer price index on Tuesday and the producer price index on Friday, looking for clues on the Fed's next move.
Check out the other names making moves in CNBC's live blog here .
While stocks are bouncing back on Monday after last week's turbulence, they may not be over the hump yet.
"With many investors unwilling to stick their neck out right before year-end, we struggle to find many positive catalysts for stocks over the near-term," said Chris Senyek, the firm's chief investment strategist, in a Monday note.
Seeing downside risks, Senyek added, "We believe markets are likely to remain very news flow driven and need to hold critical technical support levels."
Currently, the S&P 500 is trading just above its 200-day moving average.
Stocks, primarily those exposed to the AI buildout, were hit last week following a bigger-than-expected victory by Democrats in the midterm elections. But Oppenheimer chief investment strategist John Stoltzfus thinks that the market can rebound, as it started on Monday.
"So long as the underlying fundamentals that support economic growth and nurture revenue
and profit growth have not dramatically deteriorated… the market can find opportunity to not just regain lost ground but even rise well above where it had been," Stoltzfus wrote in a Monday note.
This week, he said that all eyes will be on the inflation report set to be delivered Tuesday, particularly off a hot jobs report on Friday, as investors look to predict what the Federal Reserve will do with interest rates at its December meeting. And while some investors were nervous about the AI trade following Democratic victories last week, Stoltzfus doesn't share those concerns.
"It would seem to us that it is much too early to predict the failure of AI to gain traction or achieve profitability," he said.
The New York Stock Exchange has chosen Avalanche as the primary blockchain network for processing clearing and settlement on its upcoming affiliated tokenized securities alternative trading system.
The price of the Avalanche token ( AVAX ) jumped 8%, according to CoinGecko. Shares of Avalanche Treasury Corp , which was created to be the proxy trade for the blockchain network, jumped 12% in light trading.
Avalanche is a six-year-old blockchain built for business. Unlike many networks aimed primarily at retail traders, Ava Labs, the company that helped develop Avalanche, has for years pursued financial institutions interested in tokenizing real-world assets and moving traditional financial infrastructure onto blockchain rails. Users include BlackRock, Franklin Templeton, Apollo, FIFA and the state of Wyoming.
"At the NYSE, we're looking at how blockchain technology can expand what we offer in equities, and we're picking the right technology for each job," said Dennis Lee, head of digital issuance at NYSE, said in a statement. "The upcoming digital trading platform will support equities listed on a range of blockchains, though the ledger that records and settles trades needs to be fast and reliable, let us control who can take part, keep costs predictable, and have a large community of developers behind it."
Citi is flagging the rotational turbulence beneath the index-level calm that equity markets have seen in recent days, bracing for more potential downside in the short term. The bank tactically downgraded "the US, Global Tech, and European Tech to Neutral (from Overweight)" in a Monday note.
"While fundamentals look attractive, positioning remains relatively neutral and could therefore adjust further into net short territory," Beata Manthey at Citi said. "We remain constructive on AI over the medium-term but would look for cleaner positioning and more stable AI sentiment (along with steady EPS revisions) before reestablishing our Overweight call."
U.S. equities rose on Monday morning.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 619 points, or 1.2%, shortly after 9:30 a.m. ET. The S&P 500 advanced 0.9%, while the Nasdaq Composite moved up 0.8%.
Advanced Micro Devices is on the verge of a big comeback after struggling of late, according to Oppenheimer.
The investment firm upgraded the chipmaker to outperform from perform. Its $600 price target implies 34% upside from Friday's close.
"We are raising estimates and upgrading shares of AMD on the heels of another bullish earnings call and recent fireside chat we hosted," analyst Rick Schafer said Sunday in a note to clients. "We see AMD emerging as a durable supplier of AI compute, with multi-gen customer wins and Helios rack-scale solutions supporting a materially larger [data center] business."
"Annual Instinct product cadence and [AMD's open software stack] progress strengthen AMD's competitive positioning, while compute-heavy agentic AI drives incremental [graphics processing units] and … [central processing unit] demand," Schafer said.

articles.title_orig: As War Roils Energy Markets, China Sees Its Emissions Drop
articles.title_zh: As War Roils Energy Markets, China Sees Its Emissions Drop
articles.content_orig:
Rooftop solar in Chengdu, China. Pexels
China’s carbon dioxide emissions have been flat or falling for more than two years as renewables stunt demand for fossil fuels. But the country just saw its steepest quarterly drop since the Covid pandemic, thanks to energy shocks rippling from the Iran war.
Between July and September, China saw its carbon dioxide emissions fall by 3.1 percent, according to an analysis of official figures and commercial data by Carbon Brief . That is the biggest quarterly decline since the 2022 pandemic lockdowns.
The analysis finds oil use fell by 4 percent, year on year, as Chinese drivers flocked to electric vehicles at a time when the Iran war is driving up the cost of fuel. Electric cars accounted for two in three new passenger vehicles sold in China in September, according to industry data . The uptake of electric cars has helped China ramp down oil imports in the wake of the conflict, analysts find .
Emissions from coal, meanwhile, fell by 3 percent, year on year, as the rapid growth of renewables far outstripped the rise in power demand. China added enough wind, solar, and nuclear generation over the same period to power Germany and more than twice as much as needed to meet China’s growing demand. Emissions from the production of steel and concrete also fell amid the ongoing construction slowdown.
China is continuing to build new coal plants despite the decline in coal generation. As the number of generators grows and the use of coal power declines, the average plant is seeing its running hours drop.
The shift from coal to renewables comes even as large volumes of solar and wind power go unused. China is now generating much more clean electricity than its power grid can handle. In the first six months of this year, China rejected roughly a quarter of its wind and solar output.
Analysts say that China lacks the transmission infrastructure necessary to ferry abundant clean energy from where it is generated to where it is needed. Also at issue is a policy that guarantees the purchase of electricity from newly built coal power plants.

articles.title_orig: Salsa Fargo 32 Review: An Intriguing First Move for 32-Inch Gravel
articles.title_zh: Salsa Fargo 32 Review: An Intriguing First Move for 32-Inch Gravel
articles.content_orig:
32-inch wheels offer more stability and better traction than 29-inch wheels
The geometry is well suited to handle the added weight and bulk of bikepacking equipment
Well-made and lightweight metal frame, considering the added dimensions of 32-inch wheels
High front end that makes aggressive riding positions impossible.
Slack head tube that prioritizes stability at the expense of precision.
Long wheelbase that can make the bike feel like it lumbers up to speed.
The Salsa Fargo 32 was the first 32-inch gravel bike to hit the market after it was unveiled at Sea Otter in the spring. The new Fargo is touted as a bikepacking-specific bike, which means it is a longer, slacker design than most gravel bikes.
Those qualities also let Salsa tackle some of the challenges of 32-inch gravel bike design, while avoiding other, thornier geometry problems. Conveniently, that produces a platform that is well suited for bike packing. The slack head tube, long chainstays, and tall front end all offer distinct benefits to going long into unknown terrain. The 32-inch wheels also offer benefits, smoothing over some of the bumps and rough surfaces without adding the complications of a suspension system.
Nevertheless, in our testing, we primarily rode the bike as a straight-up gravel bike. For that use case, we quickly learned just how many pros and cons arise from the new wheel size standard.
What I love about the Fargo 32 is that it exists! This is a bit of a tongue-in-cheek answer, but I mean it genuinely. If we as an industry are going to sort through what to make of 32-inch gravel bikes, we need 32-inch bikes to ride. And to be the first to market with a genuine, mainstream product is a risk, so big kudos to Salsa for that.
In riding the bike, what I noticed straight away more than anything was better traction. Talk about rollover and stability all you want, traction is where the bike had the most tangible improvement over the other bikes in our Field Test . Since we were able to standardize tires across the range of the bikes we were testing, I noticed straight away how differently the tires were handling the mix of dirt, rock, and roots I encountered on the ride. I could really dig into turns and push the bike downhill with confidence. Braking traction stood out in particular as a huge benefit to the bigger wheels.
On paper, the number-one argument for 32-inch bikes is not traction. Roll-over and efficiency over rough terrain are most frequently cited as the biggest upside of 32-inch gravel. In our testing, I was a bit let down at first. It didn’t exactly feel smooth over many of the bumps that I thought it would. Yet, I think my expectations were too high. Thirty-two-inch wheels do not have suspension, after all.
After I got more time riding the Fargo, I found that roll-over benefit to be a bit more nuanced, presenting itself in more subtle ways. We rode a steep uphill trail that was punctuated by a tough rooted step-up three times with three bikes on our first impressions day . After failing the previous two reps, I cleaned the roots with relative ease on the 32-inch bike. The increased stability, increased contact patch, and the better roll-over all worked together to smooth out the roots, allowing me to power over the feature.
That, paired with the bike’s ability to take a few seconds off my downhill time without feeling like I was risking anything, left me with a great first impression of the Fargo, even if it didn’t quite sweep me off my feet as much as I thought it would.
Those roll-over gains were further backed up in the climbing challenge, through a short, technical ascent where I was able to tackle a mix of gradients and surfaces. Despite the bike not being the lightest, nor the snappiest, the Fargo won the challenge. When I pushed uphill, the bike just held speed over things that bogged down every other option except the drop-bar mountain bike. I wasn’t able to be as precise in placing my front wheel; it didn’t matter. The bike would keep rolling.
It never really felt smooth, but that didn’t matter. It got the job done, and it preserved forward momentum better than the rigid 700c bikes, without a doubt.
All of my issues with the Fargo relate to the inability to get into a true gravel bike position. For some, this simply won’t be an issue. Plenty of riders love the upright position that the bike requires. But for me, the front end was too high even though the bike was sized correctly.
The biggest aspect that limits Salsa’s ability to get the front end of the bike lower is the same aspect that has limited many early 32-inch bikes. Compared to 700c gravel bikes, where there are many carbon fork options to build steel or titanium frames around, there haven’t been 32-inch gravel forks to work with. Instead, early 32-inch gravel bikes have used rigid 29-inch mountain bike forks.
Those forks easily fit the bigger 32-inch wheels, but they have a much higher axle-to-crown length than necessary. That excessive axle-to-crown pushes the stack higher, forcing a higher riding position. There is a limit to how short a bike’s head tube can be.
That upright position is difficult in its own right, but with the added length and slack front end, the bike is not aggressive at all. The larger wheels certainly don’t make the frame feel any snappier. The result is the bike feels like it lumbers up to speed and struggles to hold pace on calm or smooth terrain.
From an ease-of-use perspective, the Fargo 32 is fairly traditional. As you can expect from a bike-packing-centered bike, the frame is built to be configured in a few different ways. All the cables and hoses are externally routed. The seatpost has a conventional 27.2mm seatpost with dropper post compatibility. On the front end, the fork is suspension-corrected. Altogether, the bike has been built to be a modular 32-inch bike built for riders to explore 32-inch wheels on their own terms.
One of the trickier aspects of the move to 32-inch gravel bikes is the lack of a solidified standard for thru-axle spacing. The Fargo 32 uses 110mm Boost front spacing and 148mm Boost rear spacing.  That mix-and-match is key to knowing if you are looking for the right wheelset.
The Fargo 32 is a bike that is great for those looking to go far and those chasing unknown terrain. The bike is not made for speed, but certainly comes into its own the longer the ride. Its relaxed geometry makes it easy to handle, even after a long day. The improved traction from the 32-inch tires provides a bigger margin for error when things get rowdy, another benefit for riders taking on long hauls.
More than anything, what the 32-inch wheels provide the Fargo is a wheel system that can handle whatever is thrown at it. Even compared to suspension, which will always be a little bit wonky on pavement, the bigger wheels just make for a bike that can keep its head above water when things get unpredictable. In bikepacking, where even refined routes can get hairy quickly, that extra capacity can be a huge benefit.

China’s Foreign Ministry stated that the objective of these meetings is to review bilateral relations and regional developments in the Middle East.
According to a statement from the ministry, Zhai Jun referenced the widening regional conflict, emphasizing that the use of force is not a solution and that the sovereignty and security of nations must be respected.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's stock slides as questions swirl around Jensen Huang's future as CEO
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's stock slides as questions swirl around Jensen Huang's future as CEO
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's stock price dropped in early trading on Monday amid questions about CEO Jensen Huang's future at the chipmaker, following the board of directors' investigation into allegations that China targeted him in an intelligence operation.
The investigation is raising concerns about Huang's role at the company, which he co-founded and helped build into the world's second-most valuable company, with a $4.5 trillion valuation. Nvidia is barred from selling its high-end chips, specifically designed to power artificial intelligence models, to China due to competitive concerns.
Nvidia shares sank by $10.40, or 5.7%, to $176.24 shortly after markets opened, shrinking the chipmaker's market valuation by about $247 billion.
The allegations center around reports that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency. On Sunday, Nvidia's board said it is starting an "independent investigation" into the allegations, sparking questions about the CEO's future with the company.
"This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons," Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note. "The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?"
Ives added, "There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation, and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally."
Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
The company's board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."
The Chinese government dismissed allegations that it targeted Nvidia's chief executive, who co-founded the company in 1993, as part of an espionage operation. "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear," Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a statement.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a former executive at a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed International, whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Replacing Jensen Huang, 63, would prove challenging because he is viewed as integral to the company's success, tech analysts said on Monday. Huang also serves as the public face of Nvidia, appearing at industry events and media interviews in his trademark black leather jacket.
Huang is the company's fifth-largest shareholder, with about 3.4% of its shares, according to financial data provider FactSet.
"There is no known succession plan, and there is no leader in the company who would be the clear next step if he had to step down. In many ways, Jensen is Nvidia's Steve Jobs," said Daniel Newman, CEO of tech consulting firm Futurum, in an email.
He added, "That does not mean they cannot find a Tim Cook in the future, but it would be a massive changing of the guard, and the company has not been set up for that."
The scandal puts more pressure on Nvidia shares, which have already been bruised by mounting investor concerns about the valuations of companies driving AI growth. Prior to Monday's early decline, Nvidia's shares had tumbled almost 20% over the last month amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks.
The board investigation into Huang could loom over Nvidia and raise the risk that U.S. regulators could impose additional restrictions on the company's chip exports, according to Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge.
"The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised," said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.
In recent years, Jensen Huang has lobbied federal authorities to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China, winning approval from President Trump to sell its H200 chips this year. Those chips are not Nvidia's most advanced models, but they are still considered important products for Nvidia.
Previously, Huang also lobbied Mr. Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.
"The real potential fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal will be the U.S. government imposing dramatically more draconian restrictions on sales of sophisticated chips to China (the issue isn't the H200 but instead the fact that a large amount of higher-end Nvidia products are still making it into the hands of Chinese buyers)," Crisafulli said in a research note.
Agence  France-Presse and The Associated  Press contributed to this report.
